title: Interconnector Capacity Between Malaysia and Singapore: 2026 Outlook
abstract: A professor of energy systems walks through the arithmetic of cross-border electricity trade and what it means for data centre load growth in the region.
body:
## Introduction

I have spent the better part of the last decade modelling grid load in Southeast Asia, and I keep returning to one number: the capacity of the interconnectors between Malaysia and Singapore. As of 10 June 2026, that capacity stands at 1,000 MW, split between two 500 MW links. I want to walk you through the arithmetic of why this matters, especially for the data centre boom that is reshaping both grids.

Let me start with the basics. Singapore imports electricity from Malaysia via two interconnectors: one 500 MW link at Senoko and another 500 MW link at Jurong. These are not new; they have been in place for years. But what is new is the scale of demand. Singapore's data centre capacity is expected to reach 1,500 MW by 2027, according to the Energy Market Authority. That is a lot of load, and it is growing faster than domestic generation can keep up.

## The Arithmetic of Interconnector Capacity

Let us do the math. Singapore's peak demand in 2025 was about 8,000 MW. The interconnectors can supply 1,000 MW, which is roughly 12.5 percent of peak. That sounds modest, but it is critical for two reasons. First, it provides redundancy. If a large generator trips, the interconnectors can import power almost instantly. Second, it allows Singapore to tap into Malaysia's generation mix, which is currently about 40 percent coal, 30 percent natural gas, and 30 percent hydro and other renewables, according to the Energy Commission of Malaysia.

Now, consider the data centre load. A typical hyperscale data centre consumes 30 MW. If Singapore adds 500 MW of new data centre capacity by 2027, that is equivalent to about 17 new hyperscale facilities. The interconnectors can cover 1,000 MW, so they could theoretically support all of that new load and more. But here is the catch: the interconnectors are already used for other purposes, including balancing and emergency support. So the available capacity for firm imports is less than 1,000 MW.

I often ask my students to calculate the utilisation rate. In 2025, the interconnectors ran at an average of 60 percent utilisation, according to data from the ASEAN Power Grid initiative. That means about 600 MW was flowing on average. If data centre demand adds 500 MW of baseload, the interconnectors would need to run at 110 percent of their average utilisation, which is impossible without upgrades. So the question becomes: how do we increase capacity?

## Upgrades and New Links

There are two proposed projects. First, the Malaysia-Singapore interconnector upgrade, which would increase capacity from 1,000 MW to 2,000 MW by 2028. This involves upgrading the existing 500 MW links to 1,000 MW each. Second, a new 1,000 MW link via Batam, Indonesia, which is part of the ASEAN Power Grid. That project is slated for 2030. As of 10 June 2026, neither has broken ground, but the feasibility studies are complete.

Let me show the arithmetic for the upgrade. If we double capacity to 2,000 MW, and average utilisation remains at 60 percent, then average flow becomes 1,200 MW. That would comfortably cover the 500 MW of new data centre load, leaving 700 MW for other uses. But we must also consider the cost. The upgrade is estimated at USD 500 million, according to a 2025 report by the Asian Development Bank. That works out to USD 500,000 per MW of new capacity. For comparison, a new combined-cycle gas turbine costs about USD 1 million per MW. So the interconnector upgrade is half the cost of new generation.

However, there is a catch: the interconnector is only as good as the generation behind it. Malaysia's grid has its own constraints. Peninsular Malaysia's peak demand in 2025 was 20,000 MW, and its reserve margin is about 20 percent, according to the Energy Commission. That means there is about 4,000 MW of spare capacity. So Malaysia can theoretically supply the 1,000 MW to Singapore without breaking a sweat. But if Malaysia's own demand grows at 3 percent per year, as it has for the past decade, then by 2030, peak demand will be about 23,000 MW, and the reserve margin will shrink unless new plants are built.

## The Role of Data Centres

Data centres are not like typical load. They are flat, meaning they consume the same amount of power 24/7. That is both a blessing and a curse. A blessing because it is predictable, so grid operators can plan for it. A curse because it does not follow the sun, so it cannot be easily matched with solar generation. In Singapore, where land is scarce, solar potential is limited to about 2 GWp by 2030, according to the Solar Energy Research Institute of Singapore. That is only enough to meet about 10 percent of peak demand. So data centres will rely on imported power or natural gas.

I was recently asked by a policy analyst: can the interconnectors handle a 1,000 MW data centre campus? My answer was: not today, but possibly by 2028 if the upgrade proceeds. Let us do the math. A 1,000 MW campus would require the full capacity of the existing interconnectors, leaving nothing for contingency. That is unacceptable from a reliability standpoint. With the upgrade to 2,000 MW, a 1,000 MW campus would use half the capacity, leaving 1,000 MW for other uses. That is more reasonable.

But there is another issue: the interconnectors are alternating current (AC) links, not high-voltage direct current (HVDC). AC links have stability limits. The maximum power transfer across an AC link is limited by the angle difference between the two ends. In practice, the 500 MW links can transfer about 500 MW each, but if you try to push more, you risk voltage collapse. So upgrading to 1,000 MW per link is not as simple as replacing a transformer; it may require converting to HVDC, which is more expensive. The USD 500 million estimate I mentioned earlier assumes AC upgrades, but if HVDC is needed, the cost could double to USD 1 billion.

## Conclusion

As of 10 June 2026, the interconnector capacity between Malaysia and Singapore is 1,000 MW. That is enough to cover about 12.5 percent of Singapore's peak demand, but not enough to support the projected data centre growth without upgrades. The proposed upgrade to 2,000 MW by 2028 is a step in the right direction, but it faces technical and economic hurdles. My advice to policymakers is to treat the interconnectors as a bridge, not a solution. Ultimately, Singapore will need to build more domestic generation, likely natural gas with carbon capture, or import hydrogen. But for the next five years, the interconnectors are the cheapest option we have. And as any energy systems professor will tell you, the cheapest option is usually the one you already have.
